slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
An assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal: 15-minute delivery from nine dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City
Decision required: the board (two founders, two investors)
Prepared from the board briefing pack only; all figures come from the pack or are calculated from it

slides.title: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business instead

paragraphs.text: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business instead
Our own data says the orders lose money

At the median of the 14 dark stores our software already runs, each order loses $6.17 after store costs ($2.67 before them). Even the best observed value for every input, combined, still loses $1.76. No site has ever achieved that combination.
The plan needs four records broken at once

The founders' +$2.02 per order needs a $45 average order, 3.5 orders per rider-hour, 1,800 orders a day and promotions at 2%. Each is beyond anything a site has achieved. The Columbus pop-up fell short of the benchmark median on all four, losing $12.57 per order.
It breaks the cash rule even if it works

Spending $9.5M of $12.0M leaves $2.5M at month 18. That is about 6 months of runway at today's burn, half the 12-month floor. At median economics, nine stores would lose ~$18M a year, and a new round is 'unlikely'.
Software is the cheaper way to catch the same growth

Nine late-stage deals are worth $0.86M ARR (+21%), at 81% gross margin, for $0.8M a year of hires. Pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which is something we can sell them rather than compete with.
Decisions asked of the board: (1) decline Parcelbird Now as proposed; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for software hiring; (3) agree the evidence that would reopen the operator question (p. 12).
Source: Board briefing pack §§3, 6, 7, 9, 10; Parcelbird analysis. Store cost = dark-store fixed cost per order ($1.15M a year ÷ orders per year).

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing ~40% a year, but the operators already in it lose money on every order

paragraphs.text: Quick commerce is growing ~40% a year, but the operators already in it lose money on every order
Growth is real. Profit is not.
The national leader, at $1.2B of revenue, still loses $1.90 on the average order.
The one regional operator closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.
'Nobody owns the Midwest' may say more about the economics than about an open opportunity.
Compound growth 2022–25: 42% a year, consistent with the founders' 'over 40%'.
Source: Board briefing pack §5, Tables 1–2. EBITDA margin = EBITDA ÷ revenue (calculated).

slides.title: At the median of the 14 dark stores our software runs, each order loses $6.17, and $2.67 even before paying for the store

paragraphs.text: At the median of the 14 dark stores our software runs, each order loses $6.17, and $2.67 even before paying for the store
Contribution per order at benchmark-median inputs, $
The software edge is already in these numbers
These 14 stores run on Parcelbird software. Running our own stores would not add an advantage they lack.
Rider cost alone sinks the order
At $7.40, riders cost more than the goods margin after picking ($6.08).
To break even before store costs at a $34 order would take 3.75 orders per rider-hour. The observed range is 1.9–3.0.

Source: Board briefing pack §6, Table 3 (benchmark median of 14 customer sites, 2025); Parcelbird analysis. Rider cost per order = $17.75 per hour ÷ 2.4 orders per rider-hour. Store cost = $1.15M ÷ (900 × 365).

slides.title: The plan's +$2.02 per order rests on four assumptions holding at once, each beyond anything a site has achieved

paragraphs.text: The plan's +$2.02 per order rests on four assumptions holding at once, each beyond anything a site has achieved
Median to plan: contribution per order after store cost, $
Each plan input against what has actually been seen
The best order value and the best density came from different sites. No site has achieved both.
What the board is really being asked to underwrite
The plan survives missing any one target (+$0.22 to +$1.52 per order). But it needs all four together, at levels no site has reached, in cities where density is the biggest open question (§12).

Source: Board briefing pack §6, Table 3 and note; Parcelbird analysis. Bridge applies the plan's inputs one at a time in the order shown; values are contribution per order after store cost; steps may not sum exactly due to rounding.

slides.title: Even if every store matched the best observed value on every input, Parcelbird Now would at best break even per order

paragraphs.text: Even if every store matched the best observed value on every input, Parcelbird Now would at best break even per order
Contribution per order after store cost, $
* AOV $42, 3.0 orders per rider-hour and 1,400 orders a day are each the best seen, but at different sites. No site has combined them.
Only the founders' plan turns positive. The gap between 'best ever seen' (−$1.76) and the plan (+$2.02) is $3.78 per order. That is worth about $20M a year across nine stores.

Source: Board briefing pack §§6–7; Parcelbird analysis. Nine-store result = contribution after store cost × orders per day × 365 × 9 (steady state, before launch marketing and head-office cost). Pop-up uses its own $650k annualised site cost.

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up fell short of the benchmark median on all four drivers the plan depends on

paragraphs.text: Our own Columbus pop-up fell short of the benchmark median on all four drivers the plan depends on
Demand is real, but it was bought
weekly order growth (about 180 → 410 orders a day)
of order value given away in promotions, twice the benchmark
of customers still ordering in month 3, against 44% in the survey saying 'weekly'
to acquire each customer (paid social and first-order credits)
Fair caveat: a six-week temporary site is not a mature store. But even the estimated final-week rate (~410 orders a day) is under half the benchmark median and under a quarter of the plan.
Even at the plan's +$2.02 per order, a $38 customer must place ~19 orders to pay back. Retained customers order 3.1 times a month. At pop-up or median economics, payback never comes.

Source: Board briefing pack §§7–8; Parcelbird analysis. Weekly run-rates assume steady 18% weekly growth across the six weeks (11,800 orders in total). Payback counts only contribution after store cost and ignores churn after month 3.

slides.title: The one profitable example, Zipcart's densest city, got there by charging customers more, and lost 14% of its volume

paragraphs.text: The one profitable example, Zipcart's densest city, got there by charging customers more, and lost 14% of its volume
What the investor update said, and what it left out
Applying Zipcart's levers to our own benchmarks, per order
Zipcart contribution per order in its densest city, Q4 2025
A new $3.99 service fee on every order
Promotions cut to 1% of order value
Order volume in that city then fell 14%
Pricing is the only lever with evidence behind it, and it is untested here
Across the whole company, Zipcart still loses $1.90 per order
At median density, even Zipcart's pricing leaves each order losing about $1.
The founders' plan cuts promotions to 2% but adds no service fee. It also assumes volume 29% above the best site, where Zipcart's pricing cost it 14% of its volume.
It works only alongside best-ever order value and density, which no site has combined.
Whether customers keep ordering at higher prices is the open question in §12.

Source: Board briefing pack §11 (founders' investor update; Zipcart shareholder letter); Parcelbird analysis. 'Zipcart levers' = add a $3.99 fee per order, cut promotions to 1% of AOV, and cut orders per day by 14%. Other inputs unchanged.

slides.title: Even on plan, Parcelbird Now breaks the 12-month runway rule. On benchmark economics it would use up the cash

paragraphs.text: Even on plan, Parcelbird Now breaks the 12-month runway rule. On benchmark economics it would use up the cash
runway at month 18 if everything goes to plan, half the 12-month floor. That is $2.3M short.
lost by nine stores at benchmark-median economics, 1.5× all the cash we have. Losses would be about $1.5M a month.
The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator 'unlikely in this market'.
The $9.5M assumes the plan's economics. Any shortfall comes straight out of runway.

Source: Board briefing pack §§1, 3, 9; Parcelbird analysis. We assume the $9.5M covers the whole company to month 18, the most generous reading. If it excludes today's $0.4M a month burn, the need is ~$16.7M, more than the cash.

slides.title: Two further risks are not priced into the plan: rider pay rules and conflict with our own software customers

paragraphs.text: Two further risks are not priced into the plan: rider pay rules and conflict with our own software customers
Rider pay rules could move against us
Becoming an operator puts us in competition with our customers
Two of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.
Our benchmark data comes from 14 customer sites. Using it to compete with those customers puts their trust at risk.
Riders are already the biggest cost per order: $7.40 at the median, $5.07 in the plan.
Of 37 grocers in the pipeline, several want to launch fast delivery from their own stores. Parcelbird Now would compete with them in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City.
Every +$1 an hour in rider cost takes $0.29 to $0.42 off each order (plan to median productivity). At the plan's volume across nine stores, that is about $1.7M a year.
Founder time and engineering would be split between running stores and selling software, just as nine late-stage deals need closing.
The plan has no allowance for this.
Both risks grow with every store we open, and neither is costed in the $9.5M. Better operations cannot remove either of them.
Source: Board briefing pack §§6, 10, 12; Parcelbird analysis. Sensitivity = $1 ÷ orders per rider-hour.

slides.title: The software business is a cheaper way to ride the same growth: nine late-stage deals would add ~21% to ARR for $0.8M a year

paragraphs.text: The software business is a cheaper way to ride the same growth: nine late-stage deals would add ~21% to ARR for $0.8M a year
ARR from 9 late-stage deals, +21% on today's $4.1M
ARR if all 37 pipeline grocers signed (upper bound)
gross margin, on a business already growing 60% a year
a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, the whole cost
−$6.17 per order at the benchmark median
Breached, even on plan (~6 months left)

Insight: delivering from grocers' existing stores avoids the $1.15M-a-year dark store. At median density that store costs $3.50 per order, the biggest single line separating a loss from break-even. That is the product our pipeline is asking for.
Source: Board briefing pack §§1, 6, 10; Parcelbird analysis. Pipeline values = deals × $96,000 average contract; close rates are not in the pack, so the full pipeline is an upper bound.

slides.title: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, fund the software plan, and agree what would reopen the question

paragraphs.text: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, fund the software plan, and agree what would reopen the question
What would reopen the operator question
Decline the Parcelbird Now launch (nine dark stores, $9.5M) for 2027.
All three, ideally shown first by a customer's site on our platform, at no cost to us:
Approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, focused on closing the 9 late-stage deals.
Positive contribution after store costs for two quarters in a row at a site in a mid-size city doing 1,400+ orders a day
Evidence that customers accept higher prices, e.g. a service fee test where order volume holds
Commission a plan for a fast-delivery-from-store module for pipeline grocers, to come to the next board.
Funding that keeps 12+ months of runway through the launch, plus clarity on rider pay rules in Indianapolis and Kansas City
Hold cash to the 12-month runway floor. Revisit only through the triggers on the right.
Waiting costs us little. Our software already shows us how every customer site performs. If a customer's dark store starts to make money, we will see it early in our own data.
Source: Board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis. 1,400 orders a day is the best density seen at any site (Table 3); pricing evidence on p. 8.

slides.title: Appendix B: judgment calls and limits of this analysis

paragraphs.text: Appendix B: judgment calls and limits of this analysis

Definition of contribution. The pack does not define the founders' 'contribution profit'. We show results both before and after the dark-store fixed cost. The conclusion holds either way: at the median an order loses money even before the store is paid for.

Cash need. We read the $9.5M as the total company need to month 18, which is the most favourable reading for the plan. If it is on top of today's $0.4M a month burn, the plan needs ~$16.7M, more than the $12.0M in the bank.

Pop-up ramp. Run-rates of ~180 and ~410 orders a day assume steady 18% weekly growth over six weeks. The pop-up was a temporary site with a lower $650k fixed cost, so it is evidence on demand and operations, not on mature-store economics.
Customer payback. Payback uses contribution after store cost per order and leaves out orders in months 1–2 and churn after month 3, because the pack has no data on either.
Zipcart comparison. We apply Zipcart's fee, promotion and volume changes to our benchmarks with every other input unchanged. Zipcart's own definition of contribution is not given.
Not modelled. Launch marketing, head-office cost and ramp-up losses (all inside the founders' $9.5M), and close rates on the software pipeline, which the pack does not give.
Source: Board briefing pack; Parcelbird analysis.
